Question: What are the reasons why we should study ethics?
Answer: Because there are lots of issues where “right” and “wrong” that are not really clear. In addition, sometimes it may be necessary to choose “wrong” because there is no “right” and maybe you are forced to choose “less wrong”. There are no degrees of honesty - either you’re honest or you’re not. But there are many degrees of behavior that are on a spectrum from good to bad, right to wrong, necessary but regrettable and so on. Ethics is the philosophy of moral behavior and examines the validity of behaviors such as the treatment of animals. Is animal research acceptable? Why or why not? If not, what if that research could save thousands of lives? What if it could save YOUR life or your child’s life? Is organ harvesting from prisoners okay? What about Death Row inmates? What if they refuse? Do they have any say? There are countless ethical questions that require examination and ethics helps us see all sides of the problem. A common and favorite ethical dilemma is the “trolley problem”. If a runaway train is going to kill one person or five and you are the only person who can choose, do you do so or let nature take it’s course? Do you allow five people to die instead of one when you could have shunted the trolley to the one? There are many variations of this problem, it’s considered one of the hardest problems that are studied and a sizable minority of ethicists refuse to even answer. The movie “Lifeboat” examines this very issue. If you are stuck in an overcrowded lifeboat and the only chance of survival means rowing 1000 miles to the nearest land but to make it you need half of the people on board to die, would you kill them so half could survive? This is an actual issue that people in lifeboats actually have to make in WW2. When does morality end and animal survival take over? If you do horrible things to survive, what kind of person are you when you are rescued? This is the issue that faced the survivors of the plane crash in the Andes who had to eat their dead friends to survive. When you come back to civilization, are you still the same person even though you are a cannibal? What about Winston Smith in “1984” who, when faced with being eaten by a hungry badger screamed out, “Do it to Julia,” the woman he loved, in order to survive. What was he after that? What kind of man, human being was he? There are any number of stories where choices must be made. By studying ethics we can learn what it takes to make those choices and how they affect us and the people around us and how everyone else sees us. Recently in China is the story of a scientist who has claimed to have cloned human beings and altered their genetics “to improve them”. No one knows who these individuals are. If they are even alive they would be in their teens by now. But other researchers have noticed mistakes in his work. What impact did that have on the children he had borne from cloning? Is it okay? There are many questions of bio-ethics we still have a hard time answering. When my neighbor’s child had liver cancer, they were able to find a “living donor” who directed their liver to the child. This means the donor is already dying and has offered up a critical part of themselves so someone else might live. The surgical team removing the liver from the dying patient still had to do the operation as if the patient might survive even though there was a 100 percent chance he would die - you can’t live without a liver. So the surgery was not done in a sloppy or careless manner as might be done on a dead donor. All the incisions and stitches had to be achieved as if the patient would survive despite taking much, much longer and risking the liver. This is a pretty clear cut ethical issue but really, what does it matter? The guy is going to die in a few hours anyway, probably will never wake up from the surgery so why not do whatever you want? Do you see the issues here? When I was a boy - and even now - I hear people who steal from stores say things like, “They are an enormous organization. They won’t miss this thing I stole.” And the people who are saying that are correct. But does that then ameliorate or even negate their wrongness? That since “it doesn’t matter, my actions are acceptable”? Ethics concern all of these things. When Tom Brady was using a partially deflated football, did that taint his victories? Did betting on games taint Pete Rose when he was playing baseball? How do you KNOW he’s not throwing the game? How do you KNOW that even subconsciously he’s not throwing the game? Ethics and ethical behavior is a wide-ranging topic. Sometimes, when faced with a moral dilemma we do not know how to act. Imagine a car wreck as described in “I, Robot” where YOU instead of the robot have to choose between one of two children to survive. How do you choose? It’s “Sophie’s Choice” in real time. By studying ethics we see how others have acted and what represents the pinnacle of ethical behavior and what is the “slippery slope” to devastation. When does euthanasia for pain relief become a method for being convenient, or worse, for profit? How do you prevent that? The study of ethics helps us exercise our mind so that we are aware of the underlying issues and the potential future impacts they could have, not just on us, but how others view us - and how society evolves.

Question: What are some of the best essays that define poetry?
Answer: Leonard Cohen was an American poet who turned to singing. He was one of the greatest treasures America ever produced when if came to poetry and song writing. I defy you to scoff at him. Although it’s always misused, his poem/song “Hallelujah” is performed as the backdrop for many television shows and even commercials. He once wrote a stunning essay on poetry that I recommend you read. Leonard Cohen's How to Speak Poetry from Death of a Lady's Man Take the word butterfly. To use this word it is not necessary to make the voice weigh less than an ounce or equip it with small dusty wings. It is not necessary to invent a sunny day or a field of daffodils. It is not necessary to be in love, or to be in love with butterflies. The word butterfly is not a real butterfly. There is the word and there is the butterfly. If you confuse these two items people have the right to laugh at you. Do not make so much of the word. Are you trying to suggest that you love butterflies more perfectly than anyone else, or really understand their nature? The word butterfly is merely data. It is not an opportunity for you to hover, soar, befriend flowers, symbolize beauty and frailty, or in any way impersonate a butterfly. Do not act out words. Never act out words. Never try to leave the floor when you talk about flying. Never close your eyes and jerk your head to one side when you talk about death. Do not fix your burning eyes on me when you speak about love. If you want to impress me when you speak about love put your hand in your pocket or under your dress and play with yourself. If ambition and the hunger for applause have driven you to speak about love you should learn how to do it without disgracing yourself or the material.  What is the expression which the age demands? The age demands no expression whatever. We have seen photographs of bereaved Asian mothers. We are not interested in the agony of your fumbled organs. There is nothing you can show on your face that can match the horror of this time. Do not even try. You will only hold yourself up to the scorn of those who have felt things deeply. We have seen newsreels of humans in the extremities of pain and dislocation. Everyone knows you are eating well and are even being paid to stand up there. You are playing to people who have experienced a catastrophe. This should make you very quiet. Speak the words, convey the data, step aside. Everyone knows you are in pain. You cannot tell the audience everything you know about love in every line of love you speak. Step aside and they will know what you know because you know it already. You have nothing to teach them. You are not more beautiful than they are. You are not wiser. Do not shout at them. Do not force a dry entry. That is bad sex. If you show the lines of your genitals, then deliver what you promise. And remember that people do not really want an acrobat in bed. What is our need? To be close to the natural man, to be close to the natural woman. Do not pretend that you are a beloved singer with a vast loyal audience which has followed the ups and downs of your life to this very moment. The bombs, flame-throwers, and all the shit have destroyed more than just the trees and villages. They have also destroyed the stage. Did you think that your profession would escape the general destruction? There is no more stage. There are no more footlights. You are among the people. Then be modest. Speak the words, convey the data, step aside. Be by yourself. Be in your own room. Do not put yourself on.  This is an interior landscape. It is inside. It is private. Respect the privacy of the material. These pieces were written in silence. The courage of the play is to speak them. The discipline of the play is not to violate them. Let the audience feel your love of privacy even though there is no privacy. Be good whores. The poem is not a slogan. It cannot advertise you. It cannot promote your reputation for sensitivity. You are not a stud. You are not a lady killer. All this junk about the gangsters of love. You are students of discipline. Do not act out the words. The words die when you act them out, they wither, and we are left with nothing but your ambition.  Speak the words with the exact precision with which you would check out a laundry list. Do not become emotional about the lace blouse. Do not get a hard-on when you say panties. Do not get all shivery just because of the towel. The sheets should not provoke a dreamy expression about the eyes. There is no need to weep into the handkerchief. The socks are not there to remind you of strange and distant voyages. It is just your laundry. It is just your clothes. Don’t peep through them. Just wear them.  The poem is nothing but information. It is the Constitution of the inner country. If you declaim it and blow it up with noble intentions then you are no better than the politicians whom you despise. You are just someone waving a flag and making the cheapest kind of appeal to a kind of emotional patriotism. Think of the words as science, not as art. They are a report. You are speaking before a meeting of the Explorers’ Club of the National Geographic Society. These people know all the risks of mountain climbing. They honour you by taking this for granted. If you rub their faces in it that is an insult to their hospitality. Tell them about the height of the mountain, the equipment you used, be specific about the surfaces and the time it took to scale it. Do not work the audience for gasps and sighs. If you are worthy of gasps and sighs it will not be from your appreciation of the event but from theirs. It will be in the statistics and not the trembling of the voice or the cutting of the air with your hands. It will be in the data and the quiet organization of your presence.  Avoid the flourish. Do not be afraid to be weak. Do not be ashamed to be tired. You look good when you’re tired. You look like you could go on forever. Now come into my arms. You are the image of my beauty.

Question: Did anybody in your family migrate to the United States legally?
Answer: All of my grandparents immigrated through East Boston in 1912. The US built an official 602,000 sq foot immigration station there in 1919. It was a 100,000 sq foot building and a fenced in area - essentially a prison. The building is still there today, it’s abandoned and was used by Bethlehem Steel as a repair area for tug boats. The ship repair facility is still there. The building is still there too, abandoned. This is what it looks like now. My Grandfather was a wealthy man who came to America on the Cymric. In the US he lost his fortune, became a rich man’s chauffeur and married the maid who immigrated through this building from Denmark around that time. My grandfather on my dad’s side, his wife and his brother and his wife came through here as well from Parma, Italy the same year. They both returned to Italy to fight for the Italian Army in WW1 before returning to the US after the war. They were all processed and became American citizens. My dad’s family moved to the North End of Boston and later to South Boston; his brother moved to Sandwich. My mom’s dad and mom took what little money they had and bought a house in Readville on the outskirts of Boston in 1917, because in those days the hospital was free for Boston resident and they knew they would have lots of kids. Their house was the first house in the neighborhood with indoor plumbing. Every other house on the street had an outhouse. The outhouses were still there when I was a child, but they were used as garden sheds by then. My grandmother’s house had a large barn and she made extra money renting it to the city as a stable for the extra fire engine horses. Boston used horse-drawn fire engines on the outskirts until 1938. When I was a little boy, all the fire horse collars and harnessess were all still there, rotting away in the stalls with rotting hoses. There was no electricity and it was scary and there were a lot of mice. A challenge for us as children was to dare another child to climb the rickety ladder to the hayloft. I never made it into the loft because I was always so scared. This is what it looks like now. It never looked this good when I was little. My aunt did no maintenance since 1947 until she died in 1992 and it looked it. We had to shovel coal for the stove so she could cook and we had to sift ashes for clinkers It was a big day when the coal truck showed up to dump a ton of coal into the cellar. My grandmother was still making soap from those ashes until 1964. It was lye soap and it burned. Their neighbor, Mr. Johnson, was a well paid civil servant who got the first telephone in the neighborhood in 1936. Everyone else had to walk 1/2 mile to the corner store to use the payphone. People were still doing that in the early 1960s when I was little. In the store, called “Downsies”, the linoleum around the phone was worn right through to the wood. The proprietor would yell at people who hogged the phone. There was no privacy. It was right next to the bread and people would lean on the bread and crush it and he would get pissed. They also has a “Western Union” sign up til about 1970 but I never saw them send a telegram or get one. The store is still there but it’s just a typical convenience store now. There was a one-pump gas station next door that had a garage where they repaired cars. No one bought gas there unless it was an emergency because the gas was really expensive. But both places were the only store for miles so they made good for a long, long time even when I was growing up. They had the only air pump for miles so we all brought out bikes there and got yelled at by the mechanic for hanging out. There were always huge puddles of oil on the ground that made rivers of rainbows into the sewers when it rained.

Question: When and why was the rubble of World War II cleared away?
Answer: Of course there were mountains of rubble after WW2 and no German men to move it - they were all tied up in PoW and DEP camps. So the women were employed to do it. They were called “Trummerfrau” or “Brick Women” and every day they lined up and stacked the bricks from blown up buildings onto pallets and shoveled and swept away the dirt. Much of the infrastructure had been burned to ash so there were really just twisted metal and stone and brick. They did this for food and a pittance. Note the women had to build their own short line hand cart railroads as well as clear the rubble. There is even a memorial to the monumental effort made by these women. Half of all German buildings were destroyed or damaged during the war generating 500 million cubic yards of rubble. The Germans had been clearing rubble since 1940. separating re-usable brick and rock from metals that could be re-smelted and of course they had almost unlimited free slave labor to do the heaving lifting so while the problem at the end of the war was enormous, the Germans had been dealing with it all along. Of course, after the war, the slaves were gone so as usual, the women picked up the slack. In July, 1943 the Allies undertook Operation Gommorah that reduced Hamburg to rubble. It was a new experience for everyone and the firebombing caused it’s own weather and tornadoes and even the oil in asphalt caught fire so even the streets were on fire. People were burned to cinders. The Germans were shocked and covered up the destruction out of the fear it would have on the population. The actual industrial impact on the German war effort was modest as the bombs missed the industrial area. Note that there is no “wood rubble” left here. The impact of this bombing is still studied. In the book “A Woman of Berlin” the author, a German female journalist, tells of how the women have to tie up their skirts and wear rags over their face to filter out the ever-flowing clouds of dust and ash and how they often would encounter bodies, weapons, unexploded bombs - and often be killed when buildings collapsed on them. And they were always under the watchful eyes of the Russians who would rape them at every opportunity. From the beginning of the invasion of the conquered lands, the Russians made Germans, primarily German women and children, fill in shell craters, first with the bodies of German soldiers and civilians, and then with rubble on top. The Russians needed good roadways to move tanks and vehicles. Of course, the bodies would rot and the rubble settle and the Russians made them keep doing it until there was a continuously passable roadway, and this happened everywhere they went. (The Russians were known to line up wounded German soldiers and run over them with tanks as well, then have the women scrape up the remains and throw them in the shell craters.) When the snow melted, the Russians found the bodies of 250,000 dead German soldiers in Stalingrad. They used the bodies to fill shell craters. Of course, the Allies also had heavy equipment and where roads and installations such as airfields were necessary, professional engineers were used to clear and repair. After all, the Allies were preparing for the next big war with the Russians. The first priority of the Allies was clearing road. Here, the Allies are using heavy equipment to open the roads through the strategic city of St Lo in France, which changed hands many times and was the most destroyed city in Europe as a result of the war with over 90 percent considered “completely destroyed”. It was ironic because St Lo was used as a place to hide and store historical records and artifacts because it was believed the beautiful city would be bypassed and never be engaged in combat. Many historical items were lost forever. I have driven through St Lo and there is absolutely no trace of any historical building or even any “old” building; the entire city looks like an American strip mall from the 1970s with a few exceptions. The clean up went on for a long, long time because of course, there were all manner of sunken ships in the harbor, unexploded mines, abandoned weapons and artillery. In one case, a Jagdtiger that lost its steering can crashed in to a building at an important junction was there, covered in graffiti, until 1948 when American engineers tried to tow it away, only to have their equipment damaged so that had to cut it up with torches. In the book “German Boy” a small child tells of coming across a German artillery position abandoned in the woods with prepared shells and equipment and starts to “play soldier” until a former German soldier comes running to drag him away from the unstable ammunition. Later, the Allies come and clear it away. Airfields had piles of German planes pushed into heaps by bulldozers at the end of runways where the piles stacked for years until German manufacturing needed the aluminum. In that same book, the author tells of how scavengers would risk being shot to crawl through the wrecked planes for copper wire and tubes to make illegal radios to sell on the black market or to look for pistols that could be sold for a fortune. Destroyed and abandoned German equipment was gathered into dumps. The metal was still valuable and the weapons contained dangerous unexploded ordnance for years after the war. German harbors were one big oil slick with sunken and capsized ships and floating bodies and all kinds of detritus including unexploded mines and ordnance that all had to be cleared to reopen the ports. Shipyards were filled with incomplete submarines. The Americans made the Germans finish some of the Type 21s for testing. Allied bombing really never stopped rapid production of the submarines or destroyed the shipyards, which was inexplicable since from the air the shipyards were enormous. And then there was the restoration of critical historical sites, such as the Frankenchirche in Dresden that was restored in 2005. Other churches were never fully restored but sprayed inside with layers of concrete to help them maintain structural integrity. When I was in Dresden there were still plenty of buildings with second-rate repair jobs held up by a wing and a prayer - but that had been in East Germany and the Russians never spared anything to help rebuild Germany. Frankenkirche in Dresden in 1958 and in 2005 after restoration. The church had been originally built in 1100AD. In many places, like Halbe, it is apparently not difficult to find weapons, bodies and explosives from that last desperate battle when the 9th Army fought to escape destruction at the hands of the Russians in the last days of the war.

Question: When did America's love affair with fast food begin and why has it continued despite its negative impact on health and the economy?
Answer: It was the Interstate Highway Act that created the fast food industry. Sure, there have always been unhealthy diners where you could get greasy eggs, toast and coffee but it took the highway system to create a series of uniform fast-food restaurants and motels. In the very old days there were no road maps and you need an Auto Club guide that told you things like “turn left at the big rock”. When the Lincoln Highway was finished in 1935 then things began to speed up. It wasn’t just rail anymore - now there were trucks moving freight long distance and salesmen and tourists and people moving to a new job. And they couldn’t trust the rip-off motels that sprung up with bed bugs and dirty rooms and restaurants the gouged prices for garbage. It didn’t take long for companies like McDonald’s and Howard Johnson’s to develop a winning, standardized recipe that gave comfort to people and drew them in HoJos was bright orange. When you saw that, you knew you would get a clean room and a good meal. When you saw the “golden arches” you knew exactly what to expect. The local motels and diners on the road and the Ma and Pa places folded up fast leaving room for more chains and more standardization and eventually, when choice disappeared, more abuse - that’s what killed Howard Johnson’s. The invention of the Drive Thru by In-and-Out Burger in 1948 completed the circle - people don’t even have to stop to rent a room if they don’t want to, they just get food they can eat while they drive and never leave the car. It gives people what they want the most - convenience. And they will sacrifice their health to get it. There were “drive-in restaurants” as early as 1921 but the two-way speaker system used by In-and-Out Burger eliminated the need for people to leave their car and for a large number of servers running in and out of the restaurant. They literally killed the drive-in restaurant for the most part until Sonic brought it back.
